newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Colonial NZ shifts to overweight in local shares.
newsitem.headline: Colonial NZ shifts to overweight in local shares.

text.p: Colonial Investment Management (NZ) Ltd said on Friday it had moved overweight in New Zealand shares in its managed unit funds in the light of last month's centre-right coalition agreement.

The Reserve Bank last month endorsed a fall in short-term rates following a centre-right coalition accord between the National and New Zealand First parties, two months after October's general election.

"The coalition agreement was positive for the equity market and neutral to mildly negative for bonds. As a result we reduced fixed interest to benchmark and increased our exposure to shares," Colonial said in a quarterly update.
"Our exposure to offshore equities was reduced during the month in favour of cash."
Colonial has four managed unit funds: CO (conservative), C1 (low equity), C2 (medium equity) and C3 (high equity).
For C0, the allocation of New Zealand shares rose to 10.6 percent at December 31 from 6.7 percent at September 30, compared with a benchmark of 7.5 percent.
The NZ fixed interest allocation was steady just under 40 percent and property at six percent, while the cash allocation was lowered to 30 percent from 35.3 percent (benchmark 20 percent).
For C1, New Zealand shares climbed to 19 percent from 14.5 percent (benchmark 15 percent), for C2 to 30.9 from 24.8 (benchmark 25 percent) and for C3 to 38.8 from 31.6 (benchmark 32 percent).
Colonial is underweight in overseas shares and fixed interest for each of the funds.

"Within fixed interest markets we think there's better value in New Zealand. In equities, we see more value in the New Zealand market post-election that we do in international markets, given how far the U.S. has gone," said Investment Strategist Tim Mitchell.

In its NZ equities sector fund, Colonial has returned 10.83 percent net of tax in the past 12 months compared with an index rise of 11.61 percent. For NZ fixed interest it returned 5.73 percent versus an index of 5.90 percent.

Mitchell said this reflected a "bad patch" in New Zealand equities in May, June and July 1996 through misjudging the timing of a monetary easing. However, for the past few months Colonial had been two to three percent ahead of the index on a gross basis.
